titre: Rashomon Reached Venice Against the Wishes of Its Own Studio
accroche: The film that introduced Japanese cinema to the West would not have gone there without an Italian importer based in Tokyo.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 10, 1951, the 12th Venice Film Festival comes to a close and its jury awards the Golden Lion to *Rashomon*, a Japanese film released the year before. Its director, Akira Kurosawa, did not even know, he would later write in his memoirs, that the film had been submitted to the festival. His studio, Daiei, had told him neither about the entry nor about the prize.

## A Film Nobody Wanted to Send

The initiative does not come from Japan. It comes from Giuliana Stramigioli, an Italian based in Tokyo, who runs Italifilm, a company founded in 1948 to import Italian films into Japan. She sees *Rashomon* when it is released, in 1950, and recommends it to Unitalia Film, the organization promoting Italian cinema, which is then looking for a Japanese film to show in Venice. She would say in 1953 that she had been struck by the film, and convinced that it would make a great stir, whatever the list of winners.

In Tokyo, enthusiasm is thin. Japanese companies take little interest in foreign festivals: paying for prints and subtitles for a distant competition seems to them like wasted money. Above all, Daiei and others judge that *Rashomon* is a poor representation of the country's cinema. The film tells of a crime through four incompatible accounts, without saying which is true. If something had to be sent, they would have preferred a film by Yasujirō Ozu. Daiei's president, Masaichi Nagata, had in fact criticized the film when it came out. The studio ends up letting *Rashomon* go, without expecting much from it.

## What This Shifts

The film that was judged unrepresentative becomes, for Western audiences, the very face of Japanese cinema. *Rashomon* is the first Japanese film to enjoy real international success; it earns about $800,000 outside Japan and opens to critics and filmmakers in Europe and America a cinema they knew almost nothing about. Its title even comes to name a phenomenon, the Rashomon effect, when several witnesses to the same event give irreconcilable versions of it.

Nagata, who did not believe in it, later claims the success. Daiei tries to repeat it with another film, hoping for a second Golden Lion. The 1951 prize thus says less about what Japan wanted to show of itself than about what an outside gaze saw in it. The gateway to an entire cinema was chosen by an importer of foreign films, against the wishes of those who produced it.

carte.punch: Rashomon won Venice in 1951 without Kurosawa knowing that the film had been entered.
carte.idee: Its studio, Daiei, judged Rashomon unrepresentative of Japanese cinema and did not want to pay for prints for a foreign festival. It was an Italian importer based in Tokyo, Giuliana Stramigioli, who got it selected. Golden Lion on September 10, 1951.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The film's production, its reception in Japan and then abroad, and the birth of the expression “Rashomon effect.”

quiz.question: Why did Rashomon almost never get shown at the Venice Film Festival in 1951?
choix: Kurosawa refused to have his films shown outside Japan
American occupation censorship banned its export
The festival accepted no films from Asia at the time
Its studio judged it unrepresentative and balked at paying to send it
quiz.explication: Kurosawa refused nothing: he did not even know about the entry. Neither an export ban nor a festival rule played a part. The reluctance came from Daiei, which found the film unrepresentative of Japanese cinema and saw the prints and subtitles as a pointless expense.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is Giuliana Stramigioli, who set in motion the selection of Rashomon at Venice?
choix: A Japanese film critic living in Rome
The president of the Venice Film Festival in 1951
An Italian based in Tokyo who runs Italifilm
An actress who appeared in Rashomon
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text presents her as an Italian based in Tokyo who runs Italifilm, a company founded in 1948 to import Italian films into Japan.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Masaichi Nagata, president of Daiei, do after Rashomon's Golden Lion?
choix: He claims the success of the film he had criticized
He resigns as president of Daiei
He bans the film's screening in Japan
He hires Stramigioli as a producer
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that Nagata, who did not believe in it and had criticized the film when it came out, later claims the success of Rashomon.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the “Rashomon effect,” an expression born from the film's success?
